calls.reason: The Stanford/ADP study finds no economy-wide displacement but a 19% employment gap for young workers in AI-exposed jobs, and its authors call that descriptive, not causal. Yale Budget Lab finds stability. Mixed evidence and no deadline.

OpenAI's own price schedules show clear API price cuts, which undercut 'isn't getting cheaper' on a customer-price reading. But the claim's main thrust is a value judgment, and prices say nothing about providers' own costs.

The freelance-postings study (data to July 2023) and the Census survey on AI broadly both predate the target period, and neither looks at early-career creative work. They fit the claim but do not test it.

The cited paper shows exponential data needs per gain for multimodal concepts, but it does not measure money spent. Chinchilla points the other way on compute. Nothing ties equal performance gains to exponentially rising cost.

Microsoft's 10% drop in January 2026 and a shareholder suit over AI spending fit the kind of punishment described, but no source by the evaluation date reports the AI bubble collapsing, and no deadline was given.
AlphaFold 3 and Be My AI's usage count against the claim, and the weak SWE-bench results count for it. No representative comparison of the period exists, and 'very little' has no threshold.
